note: Ready-to-add effects. Each entry is a BEAT (or layer) in the engine's own grammar with its variable parts named in `params`. `scripts/add-effect.mjs` stamps one into a reel.json; nothing here is new engine code - every effect is an existing primitive, so a reel using them renders on any engine that has that primitive. Replicated from the owner's reference edit (25 Oct): a podcast breakdown whose effects map one-to-one onto kinds the engine already builds. Each effect carries `frame`: "overlay" sits over the footage with the speaker visible, "full" replaces him for its window, "full-dimmed" keeps him behind a dim. An edit built only from `full` effects keeps cutting away from the speaker, which is the single thing that stops it reading like a composited reference edit. Three things recorded as impossible on 25 Oct are now built: a progress arc (progress-arc), letterpress type (letterpress), and an outline on the cut-out (cutout-outline) - the last needed no engine change at all, because `matteFilter` already exposed it and the limitation was recorded wrongly. The last three gaps closed on 26 Oct with the owner's own files: his product shots, a YouTube screenshot, and - his idea, better than mine - a split made from two moments of the SAME clip rather than a second one.

word-tiles.what: A text page on grid paper: a small kicker, a big headline, a serif line under it. The reference's stacked word tiles.
word-tiles.note: Hand-written collage items need explicit x/y - the auto-stack only runs on the paper->collage path, so items with no position all land at 120,600 on top of each other.

keyword-takeover.what: One huge serif word over dimmed, blurred footage. The reference's big coloured keyword.
keyword-takeover.note: `size` auto-fits the width, so a long word shrinks rather than running off frame. 2-3 words reads best.

ring-badge.what: A glass ring badge with a number, which shrinks into a row with its label typed beside it. The reference's percentage ring.
ring-badge.note: `label` takes **bold part** markup. `labelAt` is when the badge shrinks and the label types in.
ring-badge.needs: nothing: a number and a label

box-words.what: Lines inking in word by word, one of them growing an accent box under the words as they land. The reference's highlighted box words.
box-words.note: Every line's words must be SPOKEN while the page is up or the build warns that it will lag the voice.
box-words.needs: nothing, but every line must be words SPOKEN while it is up

card-word.what: A word on a navy card in condensed serif caps. The reference's word on black.
card-word.note: This kind takes `lines`, NOT `text`. A `text` field builds an empty card with no warning.

text-behind.what: Two to four big words BEHIND the speaker, their head and shoulders cutting the letters.
text-behind.needs: reel.matte - the speaker is cut out. ~26 min per 10 s of footage on this CPU, so matteWindows + matteClip keep it to the seconds that need it

chrome-overlay.what: A Chrome Motion graphic over live footage instead of replacing the speaker; several can be on screen at once (mac-79).
chrome-overlay.note: A LAYER, not a beat: goes in reel.layers[]. Times are finished-video seconds. All five gm kinds work.

window-grid.what: A 2x2 grid of video windows landing one after another over the footage.
window-grid.note: Four video LAYERS with staggered `at`. Each needs a box; `audio: off` keeps the voice clean.
window-grid.needs: YOUR OWN CLIPS - one video file per window, in assets/
window-grid.cannot: the engine supplies none: four windows need four files.

grey-room.what: The reference's signature frame: the room drops to greyscale with a grid over it and the speaker stays in COLOUR on top, with type beside him.
grey-room.needs: reel.matte - the speaker is cut out, same cost note as text-behind
grey-room.note: `backdrop` is a CSS filter on the room only; the cut-out speaker is drawn over it unfiltered, which is what keeps him in colour.

bw-sentence.what: One sentence drops to black and white, hard cut in and out, like a grade change between shots. The reference's desaturated lines.
bw-sentence.note: Filters the whole picture for the window; there is no per-region version.

caption-plate.what: A tinted plate over the footage: a rule draws under it and two lines slide up word by word. The speaker stays on screen - this is the shape that makes an edit read like the reference.
caption-plate.note: hideCaptions is on: the plate IS the line, and a caption under it prints the words twice. Move it with --set elements.N.y; the default sits in the lower third.

progress-arc.what: A percentage badge with a progress ring that sweeps to its share as the badge lands. The reference's red 32% arc.
progress-arc.needs: nothing: a number and a percentage
progress-arc.note: `arc` is 0..100 and is the share the ring sweeps to; the value text is yours to write ("32%"). Without `arc` the badge is the plain glass disc it always was.

letterpress.what: Serif caps pressed into a paper plate over the footage - the reference's engraved AUDIENCE line.
letterpress.cannot: the effect is light and shade, so it only reads on a light or mid plate: on near-black it disappears.
letterpress.note: shadow `engrave` presses the word in, `emboss` lifts it out. Both are motion-text shadows, so any text element can use them.

cutout-outline.what: A coloured outline traced round the cut-out speaker, the rotoscope look in the reference.
cutout-outline.needs: reel.matte - the speaker is cut out. This is a REEL-level field, not a beat: it applies wherever the cut-out is shown, so pair it with text-behind or grey-room.
cutout-outline.note: `matteFilter` is a CSS filter on the cut-out. The outline is drop-shadows in 8 directions; raise the offsets for a thicker line.

reel.matteFilter: drop-shadow(3px 0 0 #C8102E) drop-shadow(-3px 0 0 #C8102E) drop-shadow(0 3px 0 #C8102E) drop-shadow(0 -3px 0 #C8102E) drop-shadow(2px 2px 0 #C8102E) drop-shadow(-2px -2px 0 #C8102E) drop-shadow(2px -2px 0 #C8102E) drop-shadow(-2px 2px 0 #C8102E)

photo-collage.what: Your own photos tiled over the footage, landing one after another. The reference's image collage.
photo-collage.needs: YOUR photos, in assets/. One image layer per tile - add it once per photo and give each its own box.
photo-collage.note: An image LAYER takes any file in the project; the collage SCENE's `image` items are different - those read library/engravings, a fixed set, which is why layers are the route for your own pictures.

ui-mockup.what: A real app screenshot across the frame with the speaker inset INTO it - him playing inside the YouTube player, as in the reference.
ui-mockup.needs: YOUR screenshot, in assets/. Two layers: the image, then a video layer boxed over the part of it the speaker should fill.
ui-mockup.note: Work the inset box out from the screenshot's own pixels: box_x = panel_x * (1080 / screenshot_width), and the same scale for y, w, h, plus wherever you place the image. `ui` draws a synthetic app instead and needs no file.

split-screen.what: Two moments side by side, full height. The reference uses two people; the owner's answer was better - cut two moments out of the SAME clip.
split-screen.needs: nothing if you split one clip: add it twice with a different --set in=<seconds> on each. A second person needs their clip in assets/.
split-screen.note: `in` seeks into the source, so the same file can show two different moments at once. Left box x 0 w 540, right box x 540 w 540, both full height.

limitations: Nothing in the reference is out of reach now. What each effect still needs from you is on the effect itself, under `needs` - photos, a screenshot, or a second clip where one is genuinely wanted.
